1-kings-16:2:0.summary: Baasha “walked in the way of Jeroboam… as he caused Israel to sin,” matching the charge.

1-kings-16:2:3.summary: “He raises the poor from the ground… to seat him with rulers,” echoing Baasha’s elevation.

1-kings-16:2:7.summary: Eli’s sons’ conduct keeps the people from serving God, loosely like causing Israel to sin.

1-kings-16:2:8.summary: David’s plea to Saul shares no specific element with the oracle to Baasha.

1-kings-16:2:9.summary: Aaron brought “so great a sin” on the people, a loose parallel to causing Israel to sin.

1-kings-16:2:12.summary: God “raised up the lowly” echoes raising Baasha from the ground only in general.

1-kings-16:2:14.summary: Jeroboam’s sin brings “destruction” on his house, the way Baasha now walks in.

1-kings-16:3:1.summary: “I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha.”

1-kings-16:3:2.summary: Corpses of transgressors in Isaiah share no specific element with the oracle against Baasha’s house.

1-kings-16:7:10.summary: God repays fathers’ sins on children, loosely matching judgment on Baasha’s house.

1-kings-16:9:21.summary: Servants “bound together a conspiracy, and struck Joash in the house of Mallo.”

1-kings-16:9:22.summary: Baasha himself seized the throne by striking Nadab; Elah now falls the same way.

1-kings-16:9:23.summary: Warning against hearts weighed down by “drunkenness” before a sudden day.

1-kings-16:31:0.why: Shows where Ahab's Baal worship eventually led the nation.

1-kings-16:31:1.summary: Jehu explicitly says “Ahab served Baal,” recalling the very service introduced here.
1-kings-16:31:1.why: Links Ahab's Baal worship to Jehu's later purge.

1-kings-16:31:2.summary: Only the word “Sidonians” is shared; the Danite spies at Laish have nothing to do with Jezebel or Baal.

1-kings-16:31:3.summary: Ahab did evil “as Jezebel his wife turned him aside,” directly explaining the marriage's effect described here.
1-kings-16:31:3.why: Shows Jezebel's influence driving Ahab's wickedness.

1-kings-16:31:4.summary: The law forbids intermarriage because a foreign wife “will turn your son away… and he will serve other gods,” exactly what happens with Jezebel.
1-kings-16:31:4.why: Shows the law Ahab's marriage violated.

1-kings-16:31:5.summary: Israel “served the Baalim” in Judges; a general apostasy formula, not specific to Ahab.
1-kings-16:31:5.why: Places Ahab within a recurring pattern of Baal worship.

1-kings-16:31:6.summary: The Thyatira prophetess is called “Jezebel,” drawing on Ahab's wife who led Israel into idolatry.
1-kings-16:31:6.why: Shows Jezebel as a lasting type of seductive idolatry.

1-kings-16:31:7.summary: Jezebel, the Sidonian queen named here, strikes down the Lord's prophets.
1-kings-16:31:7.why: Shows the persecution that followed this marriage.

1-kings-16:31:8.summary: Mentions Sidonians as past oppressors; no link to Jezebel, Ethbaal, or Baal service.

1-kings-16:31:9.summary: Jerusalem surpassing others in wickedness loosely parallels Ahab going beyond Jeroboam's sins; no shared persons.
1-kings-16:31:9.why: Idea of escalating sin beyond predecessors.

1-kings-16:31:10.summary: Solomon's foreign wives, including forbidden nations, turned his heart after idols, the same pattern as Ahab's Sidonian marriage.
1-kings-16:31:10.why: Earlier royal precedent for marriage leading to idolatry.

1-kings-16:31:11.summary: Leah's “Is it not enough” is only an idiomatic phrase; no link to Ahab, Jezebel, or Baal.

1-kings-16:31:12.summary: Records the death of Jezebel, “a king's daughter,” the Sidonian princess Ahab married here.
1-kings-16:31:12.why: Shows the end of Jezebel's story.

1-kings-16:31:13.summary: Joshua warns that intermarrying with remaining nations will become a trap; general warning, not about Sidon or Baal.

1-kings-16:31:14.summary: Israel worshiped “the Baalim” and “the gods of Sidon,” echoing Ahab's Sidonian Baal worship, though in an earlier era.
1-kings-16:31:14.why: Shows Sidonian Baal worship as an old snare.

1-kings-16:31:15.summary: Only the rhetorical “is it a small thing” idiom is shared; Isaiah addresses the house of David on another matter.

1-kings-16:31:16.summary: The sons of God taking wives shares only the act of taking a wife; no link to Jezebel or idolatry.

1-kings-16:31:17.summary: Shares only the “small thing” idiom about lawlessness; Ezekiel addresses Judah, not Ahab.

1-kings-16:31:18.summary: Nehemiah rebukes foreign marriages citing Solomon; shares the theme of foreign wives turning kings aside but not Ahab himself (range truncated).
1-kings-16:31:18.why: Later reflection on foreign marriages and royal sin.

1-kings-16:31:19.summary: Jezebel, Ahab's wife, plots Naboth's death, showing her dominance over Ahab introduced in this marriage (range truncated).
1-kings-16:31:19.why: Illustrates Jezebel's evil influence on Ahab.

1-kings-16:31:20.summary: Ezekiel's sacrifice of children to idols shares no specific element with Ahab's marriage or Baal service.

1-kings-16:31:21.summary: Jezebel, Ahab's wife, threatens Elijah after the Baal prophets are killed.
1-kings-16:31:21.why: Shows Jezebel as defender of Baal worship.

1-kings-16:31:22.summary: Moses' “Is this too little for you” is only an idiomatic echo; Korah's rebellion is unrelated.

1-kings-16:31:23.summary: “Was it not enough for you” is a shared idiom only; the shepherds' trampling is unrelated to Ahab's idolatry.

1-kings-16:31:24.summary: Israel “served the Baalim and the groves” in the judges' era; general formula of apostasy.
1-kings-16:31:24.why: Shows Baal worship as a recurring sin.

1-kings-16:31:26.summary: Solomon's foreign wives turned his heart, and he built for “Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians,” paralleling Ahab's Sidonian wife and Baal.
1-kings-16:31:26.why: Precedent of Sidonian worship entering through royal marriage.

1-kings-16:32:0.summary: Jehu gathers Baal's worshipers into “Baal's house,” the temple Ahab built in Samaria.
1-kings-16:32:0.why: Shows the fate of Ahab's Baal temple.

1-kings-16:32:1.summary: Jehu's men tore down “Baal's house” and its pillars, destroying the Samaria shrine Ahab set up.
1-kings-16:32:1.why: Records the destruction of Ahab's Baal sanctuary.

1-kings-16:33:0.summary: “The grove stood in Samaria” long afterward, apparently the grove Ahab made here.
1-kings-16:33:0.why: Shows the lasting legacy of Ahab's grove.

1-kings-16:33:1.summary: Ahab was “sold to do evil before the Lord,” restating his unmatched wickedness.
1-kings-16:33:1.why: Reinforces the verdict on Ahab's reign.

1-kings-16:33:2.summary: Manasseh “erected an altar for Baal, and made groves as Ahab king of Israel had done,” explicitly recalling this verse.
1-kings-16:33:2.why: Ahab becomes the benchmark for Judah's worst king.

1-kings-16:33:3.summary: The law commands Israel to “cut down their sacred groves”; Ahab instead made a grove.
1-kings-16:33:3.why: Shows Ahab's act reversed God's command.

1-kings-16:33:5.summary: Israel “made groves… and served Baal,” the practices Ahab introduced, in a general summary of the northern kingdom's sins.
1-kings-16:33:5.why: Shows Ahab's practices persisting until the exile.

1-kings-16:33:6.summary: Ahab “acted more wickedly than all who were before him,” the same verdict as this verse.

1-kings-16:33:7.summary: Ahab consults four hundred prophets; same king but no specific link to the grove or provocation.

1-kings-16:33:9.summary: The Lord announces that dogs will lick Ahab's blood, the destruction toward which he provoked his soul.
1-kings-16:33:9.why: Shows the judgment Ahab's provocations brought.

1-kings-16:33:10.summary: Ahab hates the true prophet Micaiah; same king, but no shared element with the grove or provocation.
1-kings-16:33:10.why: Illustrates Ahab's hostility to God's word.

1-kings-16:34:1.summary: Jesus' words never passing away parallels the fulfilment of “the Lord's word” through Joshua, but there is no specific link to Jericho.
1-kings-16:34:1.why: Illustrates the reliability of God's spoken word.

1-kings-17:1:0.summary: Jesus recalls Elijah's days “when heaven was shut” and famine came, referring to the drought announced here.
1-kings-17:1:0.why: New Testament reference to Elijah's drought.

1-kings-17:1:2.summary: John comes “in Elijah's spirit and power”; names Elijah but not this episode.
1-kings-17:1:2.why: Shows Elijah as model for the forerunner.

1-kings-17:1:3.summary: Micaiah's oath “As the Lord lives” echoes Elijah's oath form, in a prophet's vow to speak God's word.

1-kings-17:1:4.summary: Elisha swears “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand,” the identical formula Elijah uses here.

1-kings-17:1:5.summary: Paul cites Elijah pleading against Israel; same prophet, different episode (Horeb).
1-kings-17:1:5.why: Shows Elijah as intercessor against apostate Israel.

1-kings-17:1:6.summary: Jesus teaching with authority has no specific connection to Elijah's announcement of drought.

1-kings-17:1:7.summary: “Stand before the Son of Man” shares only the verb stand; not the prophetic servant formula here.

1-kings-17:1:8.summary: Elijah appears at the Transfiguration; same person but no link to this drought announcement.

1-kings-17:1:9.summary: In the third year the Lord tells Elijah He will give rain, ending the drought announced here.

1-kings-17:1:10.summary: Levites “stand before the Lord to minister,” the same service idiom as Elijah's “before whom I stand.”
1-kings-17:1:10.why: Explains the meaning of standing before the Lord.

1-kings-17:1:11.summary: Gabriel “stands before God,” echoing Elijah's description of himself as one who stands before the Lord.
1-kings-17:1:11.why: Illustrates the servant idiom of standing before God.

1-kings-17:1:12.summary: Paul speaks of “the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,” a similar self-description of service to God.
1-kings-17:1:12.why: Parallel confession of belonging to God.

1-kings-17:1:13.summary: The two witnesses “shut heaven, so that rain may not fall,” clearly modeled on Elijah's withholding of rain.
1-kings-17:1:13.why: Elijah's drought as pattern for end-time witnesses.

1-kings-17:1:14.summary: Only the place name Gilead is shared; Jephthah's war is unrelated.

1-kings-17:1:15.summary: Obadiah reports Ahab searched every nation for Elijah during the drought, a consequence of this announcement.
1-kings-17:1:15.why: Shows Ahab's reaction to Elijah's word.

1-kings-17:1:16.summary: Jeremiah is promised he “will stand before Me” and be as God's mouth, echoing the prophetic standing-before idiom.
1-kings-17:1:16.why: Illustrates the prophet's role as God's mouthpiece.

1-kings-17:1:17.summary: Elijah again swears “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand,” repeating this oath.

1-kings-17:1:18.summary: God's “As I live” oath to Zion shares only the oath idea; no link to Elijah or drought.

1-kings-17:1:19.summary: Elisha says “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand,” the same distinctive oath Elijah uses.

1-kings-17:1:20.summary: Bystanders mention Elijah at the cross; same name only, no link to the drought.

1-kings-17:1:21.summary: Peter proposes a tent for Elijah at the Transfiguration; same person, unrelated episode.

1-kings-17:1:22.summary: John the Baptist denies being Elijah; mentions the prophet but not this event.

1-kings-17:1:23.summary: Bystanders think Jesus calls Elijah; only the name links the passages.
1-kings-17:1:23.why: Shows Elijah's enduring place in Jewish expectation.

1-kings-17:1:24.summary: The disciples' wish to call down fire alludes to Elijah's later deeds, not to the drought here.

1-kings-17:1:25.summary: Questioners ask whether John is Elijah; mentions Elijah only by name.

1-kings-17:1:26.summary: Some think Jesus is Elijah; the prophet is named but this episode is not in view.

1-kings-17:1:27.summary: John is “Elijah who is to come”; links to Elijah generally, not to the drought.
1-kings-17:1:27.why: Elijah as type of the forerunner.

1-kings-17:1:28.summary: Sirach praises Elijah, whose “word burned like a torch,” matching his word controlling rain here.
1-kings-17:1:28.why: Later Wisdom reflection on Elijah's powerful word.

1-kings-17:1:29.summary: Sirach says Elijah “brought famine upon them,” directly recalling the drought announced here.
1-kings-17:1:29.why: Summarizes the effect of Elijah's oath.

1-kings-17:2:0.summary: Shares the prophetic formula of the Lord's word coming to a prophet, here Jeremiah rather than Elijah.

1-kings-17:2:1.summary: The same “word that came from the Lord” formula, applied to Jeremiah.

1-kings-17:2:2.summary: “The word of the Lord that came to Hosea” uses the same formula for a different northern prophet.

1-kings-17:2:4.summary: “The Lord's word came to Nathan” is the identical formula, but for another prophet and occasion.

1-kings-17:2:5.summary: “The word of the Lord came to Shemaiah” repeats the formula for a different prophet.

1-kings-17:3:0.summary: Baruch and Jeremiah “were hidden” from a hostile king, like Elijah hidden from Ahab.

1-kings-17:3:1.summary: The Greek-based text reads “holy ones,” not hidden ones, so the hiding link the label assumes is absent.
1-kings-17:3:1.why: Greek wording lacks the hiding link.

1-kings-17:3:2.summary: The woman flees into the wilderness to be nourished away from the serpent, loosely like Elijah hidden and fed away from Ahab.
1-kings-17:3:2.why: Pattern of God hiding and feeding His own.

1-kings-17:3:3.summary: God will “hide them in the hiding place of Thy presence,” a general theme of divine shelter.
1-kings-17:3:3.why: Shows God as protector of His servants.

1-kings-17:3:4.summary: “Go and hide… Let no one know where you are” parallels the command for a prophet to hide from a hostile king.
1-kings-17:3:4.why: Parallel hiding of a persecuted prophet.

1-kings-17:3:5.summary: The faithful wandering in deserts and caves loosely fits Elijah's hidden wilderness life.

1-kings-17:3:6.summary: Micaiah predicts someone hiding in an inner room; the shared verb hide is incidental.

1-kings-17:3:7.summary: Jesus hiding from stoning shares only the verb hide; no specific connection.

1-kings-17:3:8.summary: The woman flees to a place God prepared to be nourished, similar to Elijah's appointed refuge.
1-kings-17:3:8.why: God's prepared refuge for His people.

1-kings-17:3:9.summary: Paul being sent away to the sea has no meaningful link to Elijah's hiding.

1-kings-17:4:0.summary: “I have commanded a widow there to sustain you” repeats “I will command the ravens to sustain you there.”
1-kings-17:4:0.why: Pairs God's two provisions for Elijah.

1-kings-17:4:1.summary: God feeds “the young ravens”; here ravens instead feed the prophet, a loose shared image.
1-kings-17:4:1.why: God's care through and for ravens.

1-kings-17:4:2.summary: God prepares food for the raven; ravens and divine provision are shared, but roles reversed.
1-kings-17:4:2.why: God as provider of all creatures.

1-kings-17:4:3.summary: Living “on every word… of God” loosely fits Elijah sustained by God's command.
1-kings-17:4:3.why: Dependence on God's word for life.

1-kings-17:4:4.summary: Elijah is again miraculously fed with bread and water by the Lord's angel.

1-kings-17:4:5.summary: “He commanded, and they were created” shows creation obeying God's command, as the ravens do.

1-kings-17:4:6.summary: Job's statement about God providing quiet and hiding His face has no specific link to ravens or provision.

1-kings-17:4:7.summary: God's ordering of sea and dawn shares no specific element with the ravens' feeding.

1-kings-17:4:8.summary: Angels minister to Jesus in the wilderness, loosely like the ravens serving Elijah.

1-kings-17:4:9.summary: “I will command the dragon there” echoes “I will command the ravens… there,” but for judgment, not provision.
1-kings-17:4:9.why: God commanding creatures to do His will.

1-kings-17:4:10.summary: God provides water from a rock, a general parallel to water from the wadi.

1-kings-17:5:0.summary: Doing what Jesus commands loosely parallels Elijah acting according to the Lord's word.

1-kings-17:5:1.summary: Trusting God wholeheartedly fits Elijah's obedience, but no specific shared element.

1-kings-17:5:2.summary: Elijah lodges in a cave at Horeb, another place of hiding, but a different episode.

1-kings-17:5:3.summary: Taking up one's cross has no specific connection with Elijah staying at the wadi.

1-kings-17:6:0.summary: God giving “heaven's bread” in the wilderness parallels God's provision of bread for Elijah.

1-kings-17:6:1.summary: Not being anxious about food because the Father knows our needs fits Elijah's provision only generally.

1-kings-17:6:2.summary: Water from a rock in the wilderness loosely parallels Elijah drinking from the wadi.

1-kings-17:6:3.summary: Jeremiah receives a daily loaf while imprisoned, like a prophet sustained with daily bread.

1-kings-17:6:4.summary: “With God all things are possible” fits the miraculous feeding only as a general principle.
1-kings-17:6:4.why: God's power to do the impossible.

1-kings-17:6:5.summary: Disciples sent without provisions lacked nothing, loosely like Elijah supplied by God.

1-kings-17:6:6.summary: Jesus' feeding of the five thousand shares miraculous provision of bread, not ravens or Elijah.

1-kings-17:6:7.summary: The righteous “in days of famine… will be filled,” precisely Elijah's experience during the drought.

1-kings-17:6:8.summary: God provides water for thirsty Samson; general miraculous water provision.
1-kings-17:6:8.why: God gives water to His servant.

1-kings-17:6:9.summary: The righteous one dwells in a rocky hideout and “Bread will be given him, and his water is trustworthy,” closely fitting Elijah at the wadi.
1-kings-17:6:9.why: Promise of bread and water to the hidden righteous.

1-kings-17:6:10.summary: Those who seek the Lord “will not lack any good thing”; general provision theme.
1-kings-17:6:10.why: God provides for those who fear Him.

1-kings-17:6:11.summary: “From the eater came food” is a loose image that could fit ravens bringing food, but the riddle is unrelated.
1-kings-17:6:11.why: Paradox of food from unlikely sources.

1-kings-17:6:12.summary: Those who hope in the Lord will be pastured; general divine provision.

1-kings-17:6:13.summary: God's hand suffices to supply meat in the wilderness, loosely like meat brought to Elijah.

1-kings-17:6:14.summary: God's unchangeable oath and hope share no specific element with ravens feeding Elijah.

1-kings-17:6:15.summary: Contentment because God “will not leave you” fits Elijah's daily provision in a general way.
1-kings-17:6:15.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-kings-17:6:16.summary: Israel ate manna in the wilderness; general precedent for miraculous daily food.

1-kings-17:6:17.summary: Rejoicing in God when food fails relates to drought conditions only generally.

1-kings-17:6:18.summary: The Babylonian captain's offer to look after Jeremiah has no meaningful link to ravens feeding Elijah.

1-kings-17:7:0.summary: God's unfailing mercy despite moving mountains has no specific link to the wadi drying up.

1-kings-17:7:1.summary: Renewed strength for those enduring for God shares nothing specific with the dried wadi.

1-kings-17:8:0.summary: The Greek-based wording “The Lord Has Seen” lacks the provision idea, and the verse has no link to the word coming to Elijah.
1-kings-17:8:0.why: No real link in the Saints wording.

1-kings-17:8:1.summary: The identical phrase “The Lord's word came to Elijah” introduces the previous command.
1-kings-17:8:1.why: Repeated formula marking each new instruction.

1-kings-17:8:2.summary: God promises not to abandon those seeking water when there is none, fitting the drought generally.

1-kings-17:8:3.summary: “The Lord is my helper” has no specific link to the word coming to Elijah.

1-kings-17:9:1.summary: Obadiah names “Zarephath” as a boundary of the land, the same Sidonian town.

1-kings-17:9:2.summary: Treasure in clay jars has no specific link to the command to go to Zarephath.

1-kings-17:9:3.summary: “I will command the ravens to sustain you there” is the parallel command to “I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”
1-kings-17:9:3.why: Pairs God's two provisions for Elijah.

1-kings-17:9:4.summary: Jesus goes to the region of Tyre and Sidon and meets a Gentile woman, loosely like Elijah sent to a Sidonian widow.
1-kings-17:9:4.why: Grace to a Gentile woman in Sidon's region.

1-kings-17:9:5.summary: Abraham's faith in God who gives life shares no specific element with the command to go to Zarephath (range truncated).

1-kings-17:9:6.summary: Gideon's reduction of troops has no link to Elijah being sent to a widow.

1-kings-17:9:7.summary: Testing Gideon's men at the water has no link to Elijah's journey to Zarephath.

1-kings-17:10:0.summary: Abraham's servant asks a woman, “Give me a little water to drink,” closely matching Elijah's request.
1-kings-17:10:0.why: Parallel request for water from a woman.

1-kings-17:10:1.summary: Jesus asks a foreign woman, “Give Me a drink,” as Elijah asks a Gentile widow for water.
1-kings-17:10:1.why: Request for water opening grace to an outsider.

1-kings-17:10:2.summary: Paul's hunger and thirst in ministry loosely parallel Elijah's need for water.

1-kings-17:10:3.summary: The faithful “destitute, afflicted” fits Elijah's needy state only generally.

1-kings-17:10:4.summary: Hagar's water runs out, a loose parallel to scarcity of water and a mother in need.

1-kings-17:11:0.summary: Rebekah readily brings water to a stranger, as the widow goes at once to fetch water for Elijah.

1-kings-17:11:1.summary: God had “commanded a widow there to sustain you”; Elijah's request begins that provision.

1-kings-17:11:2.summary: Giving food and drink to the hungry and thirsty parallels the widow's service in general.
1-kings-17:11:2.why: Feeding the needy as service to God.

1-kings-17:11:3.summary: Giving a cup of water to a disciple brings reward, loosely like the widow's gift to the prophet.

1-kings-17:11:4.summary: Abraham offers bread to visitors, a general hospitality parallel.

1-kings-17:11:5.summary: Hospitality to strangers who may be God's messengers fits the widow's welcome generally.

1-kings-17:11:6.summary: Obadiah sustains prophets “with bread and water” during the same crisis, a general parallel.

1-kings-17:12:0.summary: The disciples have only a few loaves before a miracle, loosely like the widow's handful of flour.

1-kings-17:12:1.summary: The widow's “As the Lord your God lives” echoes Elijah's oath in 17:1 that caused the drought she suffers.

1-kings-17:12:2.summary: Hagar expects her child to die from want, as the widow expects she and her children “will eat and die.”

1-kings-17:12:3.summary: Eating bread with want during judgment loosely parallels the widow's scarcity.

1-kings-17:12:4.summary: A destitute widow with only oil receives a miraculous supply through Elisha, closely paralleling this episode (range truncated).

1-kings-17:12:5.summary: “The Lord lives” oath is shared, but Jeremiah condemns false swearing.

1-kings-17:12:6.summary: The “pain of famine” in Jerusalem parallels the famine the widow faces generally.

1-kings-17:12:7.summary: Abigail's “as the Lord lives” shares only the common oath formula.

1-kings-17:12:8.summary: Those wounded by famine fare worse than by sword; a general famine theme.

1-kings-17:12:9.summary: Saul's “As the Lord lives” is the same oath formula in an unrelated context.

1-kings-17:12:10.summary: Swearing “The Lord lives” in truth shares the oath formula only.

1-kings-17:12:11.summary: David's “As the Lord lives” is the same oath formula, otherwise unrelated.

1-kings-17:12:12.summary: Ittai's “As the Lord lives” shares the oath formula, with no other link.

1-kings-17:12:13.summary: Food destroyed before the eyes in Joel parallels famine conditions generally.

1-kings-17:12:14.summary: Jonathan's “as the Lord lives” shares only the oath formula.

1-kings-17:12:15.summary: The people's “As the Lord lives” oath for Jonathan is the same formula in an unrelated setting.

1-kings-17:12:16.summary: David's “as the Lord lives” and nearness to death share wording only loosely.

1-kings-17:13:0.summary: Giving first to God and testing whether He will pour out blessing “until there is enough” loosely fits feeding the prophet first.
1-kings-17:13:0.why: Giving first to God brings blessing.

1-kings-17:13:1.summary: “Seek first the kingdom… all these things will be added” parallels putting the prophet first, then receiving provision.

1-kings-17:13:2.summary: God's “Do not fear” matches Elijah's encouragement in sense only, a common reassurance.

1-kings-17:13:3.summary: Moses' “Take courage” before God's deliverance shares the phrase but a different event.

1-kings-17:13:4.summary: The angel's “Do not be afraid” to the women is a generic reassurance with no specific link.

1-kings-17:13:5.summary: Elisha's “Do not be afraid” shares a prophet's reassurance, otherwise unrelated.

1-kings-17:13:6.summary: “Do not fear” before seeing the Lord's salvation is a general reassurance parallel.

1-kings-17:13:7.summary: The angel's “Do not fear, Paul” is a generic reassurance with no specific link.

1-kings-17:13:8.summary: God testing Abraham with his son loosely parallels the widow's test of giving first.

1-kings-17:13:9.summary: Gideon's men lapping water has no meaningful link to the widow's test.

1-kings-17:13:10.summary: Honoring the Lord with firstfruits parallels giving the first cake to God's prophet only generally.

1-kings-17:13:11.summary: The tested genuineness of faith fits the widow's test in a general way.

1-kings-17:13:12.summary: Putting Christ before children loosely parallels feeding the prophet before her children.

1-kings-17:13:13.summary: Abraham's faith when tested over his son parallels the widow's faith only generally.

1-kings-17:13:14.summary: “Do not fear, for I am with you” is a general reassurance like Elijah's “Take courage.”

1-kings-17:13:15.summary: The rich young man refuses to give up his goods, contrasting with the widow giving from her little.

1-kings-17:14:0.summary: Jesus multiplies loaves for four thousand, a general parallel to food that does not run out.

1-kings-17:14:1.summary: The feeding of five thousand from five loaves parallels miraculous sufficiency generally.

1-kings-17:14:2.summary: “Thus says the Lord: They will eat and leave some over,” and it happened “according to the word of the Lord,” closely matching this promise.

1-kings-17:14:3.summary: Elisha's “Thus says the Lord” promising cheap flour shares prophetic promise of food relief.

1-kings-17:14:4.summary: “Thus says the Lord” introduces water provision in drought, a loose parallel.

1-kings-17:14:5.summary: The ravens' provision is an earlier divine supply for Elijah, but no shared promise of flour or oil.
1-kings-17:14:5.why: Prior provision in the same drought.

1-kings-17:14:6.summary: Anointing oil and “Thus says the Lord” are incidental; Jehu's anointing is unrelated.

1-kings-17:14:7.summary: A widow's oil keeps flowing until the vessels are full, a close parallel to the unfailing flask of oil (range truncated).

1-kings-17:15:0.summary: A poor widow gives sacrificially, loosely like the Zarephath widow's obedience.
1-kings-17:15:0.why: Faithful giving by a poor widow.

1-kings-17:15:1.summary: Abraham's tested obedience parallels the widow's acting on God's word only generally.

1-kings-17:15:2.summary: Noah “did all that the Lord God commanded,” a general parallel to the widow acting as told.

1-kings-17:15:3.summary: Jesus praises a Gentile woman's faith; loose parallel to the Gentile widow's trust.

1-kings-17:15:4.summary: Abraham did not waver at God's promise, a general parallel to the widow's trust.

1-kings-17:15:5.summary: Noah and Abraham act by faith on God's word, generally like the widow.

1-kings-17:15:6.summary: Abraham rises and goes as God said, loosely paralleling immediate obedience.

1-kings-17:15:7.summary: “Trust in His prophet, and you will prosper” is exactly illustrated by the widow trusting Elijah and being fed.

1-kings-17:15:8.summary: Believing to see God's glory parallels the widow's faith rewarded only generally.

1-kings-17:16:0.summary: “According to your faith, let it happen” fits the fulfilment of the Lord's word only in a general way.

1-kings-17:16:1.summary: The official believed Jesus' word and found it fulfilled, a general parallel to fulfilment “according to the Lord's word.”
1-kings-17:16:1.why: Trusting a spoken word of power.

1-kings-17:16:2.summary: “No word from God will be powerless” matches the reliability of the Lord's word here only as a principle.

1-kings-17:16:3.summary: “With God all things are possible” is a general principle behind the unfailing flour and oil.

1-kings-17:16:4.summary: “According to the word which the Lord spoke… to Jehu the prophet” uses the same fulfilment formula.

1-kings-17:16:5.summary: The altar split “according to the portent the man of God had given by the Lord's word,” the same fulfilment formula.

1-kings-17:16:6.summary: Elizabeth blesses Mary for believing in “a fulfillment of the things spoken… from the Lord,” a general parallel.

1-kings-17:17:0.summary: Lazarus' illness precedes a raising, loosely paralleling the boy's fatal illness before Elijah revives him.

1-kings-17:17:1.summary: “After these things” God tests Abraham concerning his son, a loose parallel to the widow's trial over her son.

1-kings-17:17:2.summary: Jesus announces “Lazarus died,” a general parallel to the boy's death before a raising.

1-kings-17:17:3.summary: Joy in trials testing faith fits the widow's trial only generally.

1-kings-17:17:4.summary: “The breath of every human being” is in God's hand, related to the boy's breath leaving him.

1-kings-17:17:5.summary: “Your breath is in His hand” loosely relates to the boy's breath ceasing.

1-kings-17:17:6.summary: “The body without spirit is dead” describes death as absence of spirit, loosely like no breath remaining.

1-kings-17:17:7.summary: Mourning over a firstborn in Zechariah has no specific link to the widow's son's illness.

1-kings-17:17:8.summary: Faith tested by fire shares no specific element with the boy's illness.

1-kings-17:17:9.summary: The Shunammite's son suddenly falls ill and dies, closely paralleling the widow's son before the prophet's raising.

1-kings-17:17:10.summary: The fiery ordeal of believers has no specific link to the boy's illness.

1-kings-17:17:11.summary: God “wilt take back their breath, and they will fail,” loosely like the boy's breath ceasing.

1-kings-17:17:12.summary: The crown of life for those enduring trial has no specific link to this illness.

1-kings-17:17:13.summary: If God retained the spirit all would perish; loosely relates to breath leaving the boy.

1-kings-17:18:0.summary: Peter's “Depart from me… I am a sinful man” shares a sinner's fear before God's holy agent.
1-kings-17:18:0.why: Sense of sin before a holy presence.

1-kings-17:18:1.summary: “What is this to Me and to you” echoes the idiom “What have I to do with you,” in a different context.

1-kings-17:18:2.summary: “What have we to do with Thee… Hast Thou come to destroy us?” closely matches the widow's “What have I to do with you… come… to put my son to death.”
1-kings-17:18:2.why: Same idiom with fear of destruction.

1-kings-17:18:3.summary: Elisha's “What have I to do with you?” shares the idiom only.

1-kings-17:18:4.summary: David's “What have I to do with you” shares the idiom in an unrelated setting.

1-kings-17:18:5.summary: Obadiah also asks how he has sinned and fears Elijah's coming will “put me to death,” a similar reaction.

1-kings-17:18:6.summary: Job feels God recording his sins against him, like the widow's fear her wrongs are remembered.
1-kings-17:18:6.why: Suffering read as punishment for sin.

1-kings-17:18:7.summary: Only the title “man of God” is shared; the Bethel episode is unrelated.

1-kings-17:18:8.summary: Necho's “What is there between me and you” is a similar idiom in a different setting.

1-kings-17:18:9.summary: Elders fear the arrival of the seer, a general parallel to dread at a prophet's presence.

1-kings-17:18:10.summary: Joseph's brothers seek pardon for past iniquity, loosely like guilty memories resurfacing.

1-kings-17:18:11.summary: People fearfully beg Jesus to leave, loosely like the widow's dismay at the man of God.

1-kings-17:18:12.summary: Joseph's brothers interpret their affliction as payback for past sin, as the widow sees her son's death as remembrance of her wrongs.
1-kings-17:18:12.why: Calamity awakening a sense of guilt.

1-kings-17:18:13.summary: Herod's guilty fear about John shows conscience stirred, only loosely related.

1-kings-17:18:14.summary: Ezekiel speaks of injustices recalled “for remembrance,” echoing wrongdoings brought to remembrance.

1-kings-17:18:15.summary: “What have I to do with Thee” is the same idiom, from a demon fearing torment.

1-kings-17:18:16.summary: David's “What have I to do with you” is the same idiom, unrelated situation.

1-kings-17:18:17.summary: Job asks how many his sins are, loosely like the widow linking suffering to her sins.
1-kings-17:18:17.why: Seeking cause of suffering in sin.

1-kings-17:18:18.summary: “What hast Thou to do with me” repeats the idiom from a demon pleading not to be tormented.

1-kings-17:18:19.summary: The brothers fear repayment for past evils, a loose guilt parallel.

1-kings-17:19:0.summary: Elisha finds the dead child “lying on his bed,” paralleling Elijah laying the boy on his bed.

1-kings-17:19:1.summary: Tabitha's body is laid “in an upper room” before Peter raises her, like the boy carried to the upper room.

1-kings-17:19:2.summary: The Shunammite laid her dead son “on the bed of the man of God,” matching Elijah laying the boy on his own bed.

1-kings-17:19:3.summary: The Shunammite prepares an upstairs room with a bed for Elisha, like Elijah's upper room where he stayed.

1-kings-17:20:0.summary: Believing prayer receives answers, a general parallel to Elijah's cry to God.

1-kings-17:20:1.summary: James cites Elijah's earnest prayer and says prayer will “raise him up,” directly linking Elijah and healing prayer.
1-kings-17:20:1.why: Elijah as model of effective prayer.

1-kings-17:20:2.summary: Abraham boldly questions God's justice toward the innocent, like Elijah protesting the son's death.

1-kings-17:20:3.summary: Elijah again “cried out” to the Lord in prayer at Carmel.

1-kings-17:20:4.summary: Hezekiah addresses the Lord in prayer during crisis; general prayer parallel.

1-kings-17:20:5.summary: Joshua's lament to God after disaster parallels Elijah's complaint generally.

1-kings-17:20:6.summary: Moses, Aaron and Samuel “called upon the Lord, and He heard them,” a general parallel to Elijah's cry.

1-kings-17:20:7.summary: Moses “cried out to the Lord” in distress; similar prophetic cry, different situation.

1-kings-17:20:8.summary: Samuel “cried to the Lord… and the Lord heard him,” a general prophetic intercession parallel.

1-kings-17:20:9.summary: Jeremiah argues his case with God about justice, like Elijah's protest.

1-kings-17:20:10.summary: The psalmist laments apparent injustice to the righteous, loosely like Elijah's complaint.

1-kings-17:20:11.summary: Hezekiah's request for prayer against Rabshakeh has no specific link to Elijah's cry over the boy.

1-kings-17:21:0.summary: Paul falls upon the dead youth and says “his life is in him,” paralleling Elijah's prayer for the child's soul to return.

1-kings-17:21:2.summary: Peter prays alone over Tabitha and she revives, paralleling Elijah's prayer for the dead child.

1-kings-17:21:3.summary: Abraham believed “God is able even to raise the dead,” a general resurrection faith.

1-kings-17:21:4.summary: Peter's trance while hungry has no connection to Elijah's prayer over the child.

1-kings-17:21:5.summary: Sirach says to Elijah, “You raised a dead man from death… by the word of the Most High,” recalling this miracle.

1-kings-17:22:0.summary: A spirit of life enters the dead witnesses; the Saints verse only says “It happened so, and the child cried out,” so the link is general.

1-kings-17:22:1.summary: “I will put to death, and make alive” states the principle behind the child's revival.

1-kings-17:22:2.summary: “Women received their dead through resurrection” alludes to the widow receiving her revived son.

1-kings-17:22:3.summary: Christ as Lord of dead and living is a general doctrine with no specific link to this event.

1-kings-17:22:4.summary: The dead will hear and come out; a general resurrection theme.

1-kings-17:22:5.summary: Jesus cries out to raise Lazarus; a raising parallel, but the crying out is by a different person.

1-kings-17:22:6.summary: “The Lord puts to death and gives life” states the principle at work.

1-kings-17:22:7.summary: A dead man revives touching Elisha's bones, another raising in the prophetic cycle.

1-kings-17:22:8.summary: Jesus raises a child with “Child, rise”; a raising parallel, though the Saints verse only notes the child cried out.

1-kings-17:22:9.summary: The boy is brought away alive, a general parallel to the revived child.

1-kings-17:23:0.summary: Elisha says “Take your son” and the mother receives him, closely paralleling “gave him to his mother… your son lives.”

1-kings-17:23:2.summary: Peter “presented her alive” to the widows, like Elijah presenting the living son to his mother.

1-kings-17:23:3.summary: “Women received their dead through resurrection” recalls the widow receiving her son alive.
1-kings-17:23:3.why: New Testament recollection of this miracle.

1-kings-17:24:0.summary: “Now we know… Thou didst come forth from God” parallels recognition of a man of God, generally.

1-kings-17:24:2.summary: A sign leads disciples to believe, a general parallel to the widow's faith.

1-kings-17:24:3.summary: Knowing the truth in 1 John shares only the word truth.

1-kings-17:24:4.summary: Samaritans confess Jesus as Savior, and a son is healed; loose parallels in recognition and a sick son (range truncated).

1-kings-17:24:6.summary: Ecclesiastes' “words of truth” is incidental wording with no link to the prophet's authentication.

1-kings-17:24:7.summary: Jesus' unique works as testimony relate generally to miracles validating God's agent.

1-kings-17:24:8.summary: Lazarus' death serves so that disciples “may believe,” a general parallel.

1-kings-17:24:9.summary: Jesus prays aloud so people believe He was sent, loosely like the miracle confirming Elijah.

1-kings-18:1:0.summary: Jesus speaks of Elijah's days “when heaven was shut for three years,” the drought ending here.

1-kings-18:1:6.summary: God will rain on Zion as before, a general promise of restored rain.

1-kings-18:1:14.summary: God brings clouds and rain from His treasuries, a general rain-giver theme.

1-kings-18:3:4.summary: Abraham's servant who ruled his house parallels a steward's office only.

1-kings-18:3:6.summary: Joseph as overseer of a foreign master's house parallels a godly steward serving a pagan ruler.

1-kings-18:3:8.summary: Those who feared the Lord are remembered by God; general theme.

1-kings-18:3:13.summary: The fear of the Lord gives strength; general wisdom theme.

1-kings-18:3:14.summary: “Now I know that you fear God” shares the God-fearing description only.

1-kings-18:3:15.summary: Obadiah says he “has feared the Lord from his youth,” restating this description.

1-kings-18:3:16.summary: Cornelius is “fearing God,” a general God-fearer parallel.

1-kings-18:4:1.summary: “Whoever receives a prophet… will receive a prophet's reward” fits Obadiah sheltering and feeding the prophets.

1-kings-18:4:6.summary: Israel “killed Thy prophets who testified among them,” as Jezebel struck the Lord's prophets.

1-kings-18:7:3.summary: Sarah's laughter shares only the incidental “my lord.”

1-kings-18:7:7.summary: Soft clothing in kings' houses has no specific link to this verse.

1-kings-18:7:8.summary: Abraham runs to meet visitors and bows, a general gesture of reverence.

1-kings-18:7:9.summary: David “fell on his face” before Jonathan; shared gesture only.

1-kings-18:8:0.summary: Introduces Obadiah, Ahab's steward, whose “lord” Elijah tells him to inform.

1-kings-18:8:1.summary: Instructions to honor the king and slaves to submit have no specific link to Elijah's command.

1-kings-18:8:2.summary: Paying dues and honor has no specific link to this verse.

1-kings-18:9:0.summary: The widow likewise fears Elijah's coming will bring death, saying he came “to put my son to death,” as Obadiah fears being put “to death.”
1-kings-18:9:0.why: Similar fear of the prophet's presence.

1-kings-18:9:2.summary: The foremen accuse Moses of “putting a sword into his hands to kill us,” like Obadiah fearing Elijah hands him to Ahab to die.
1-kings-18:9:2.why: Fear of being exposed to a tyrant's wrath.

1-kings-18:10:0.summary: Obadiah's oath echoes Elijah's “As the Lord… lives,” and the search stems from the drought announced there.

1-kings-18:10:1.summary: God preserving the faithful from the ungodly is too general to connect specifically.

1-kings-18:10:2.summary: The widow's “As the Lord your God lives” is the identical oath Obadiah uses.
1-kings-18:10:2.why: Same oath in the Elijah narrative.

1-kings-18:10:3.summary: The king orders the prophets seized, “But they were hidden,” as Ahab's search failed to find Elijah.
1-kings-18:10:3.why: Kings unable to find hidden prophets.

1-kings-18:10:4.summary: Elijah was sent to Sidonian territory, where Ahab's searchers apparently failed to find him.

1-kings-18:10:5.summary: God hides His own “in the hiding place of Thy presence,” a general protection theme.

1-kings-18:10:6.summary: David's “As the Lord lives” shares only the oath formula.

1-kings-18:10:7.summary: Dwelling in the shelter of God is a general protection theme.

1-kings-18:10:8.summary: The ungodly persecuting the poor has no specific link to Ahab's search.

1-kings-18:10:9.summary: Solomon's “as the Lord lives” oath shares only the formula.

1-kings-18:10:10.summary: Elijah answers Obadiah with his own oath, promising to show himself, in the same conversation.
1-kings-18:10:10.why: Elijah's reply in the same scene.

1-kings-18:10:11.summary: Elijah hid at the Chorrath wadi, explaining why Ahab could not find him.

1-kings-18:10:12.summary: Achish's “As the Lord lives” shares the oath formula only.

1-kings-18:10:13.summary: Jehoiakim sends men abroad to seize the prophet Uriah, like Ahab searching every nation for Elijah.
1-kings-18:10:13.why: King hunting a prophet across borders.

1-kings-18:10:14.summary: Jesus hiding from stoning shares only the idea of escape.

1-kings-18:11:1.summary: Obadiah repeats nearly verbatim, “Go, tell your lord, ‘Behold, Elijah is here,’” adding “He will kill me!”
1-kings-18:11:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-kings-18:12:0.summary: “The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away,” exactly the kind of removal Obadiah fears for Elijah.
1-kings-18:12:0.why: The Spirit carrying a prophet away.

1-kings-18:12:1.summary: The prophets fear “a spirit of the Lord has lifted him” and cast Elijah somewhere, the same expectation Obadiah voices.

1-kings-18:12:2.summary: A spirit lifts Ezekiel and brings him elsewhere, but in a vision.

1-kings-18:12:3.summary: The Lord's hand carries Ezekiel in vision to Israel, a general transport parallel.

1-kings-18:12:4.summary: “A spirit lifted me and brought me” to the captives, in a vision.

1-kings-18:12:5.summary: “A spirit took me up” describes Ezekiel carried by the Spirit, a general parallel.

1-kings-18:12:6.summary: The Lord brings Ezekiel out “in spirit” to the valley, a general parallel.

1-kings-18:12:7.summary: A man “caught up” to the third heaven is a loose parallel to being carried away.

1-kings-18:12:8.summary: Elijah is finally “taken up… as into heaven,” the ultimate carrying away Obadiah half-expects.

1-kings-18:12:9.summary: Saul kills priests for aiding David, like Obadiah's fear of death for his part with Elijah (range truncated).

1-kings-18:12:10.summary: Samuel's godly youth loosely parallels fearing the Lord “from his youth.”

1-kings-18:12:11.summary: Samuel's recognition as a prophet shares nothing specific with Obadiah's fear.

1-kings-18:12:12.summary: John filled with the Spirit from the womb loosely parallels lifelong devotion.

1-kings-18:12:13.summary: Herod “searched for him and did not find him” and executed the guards, the fate Obadiah fears from Ahab.
1-kings-18:12:13.why: Tyrant punishing servants when a target vanishes.

1-kings-18:12:14.summary: “The one who fears God will come through them all” loosely encourages Obadiah's situation.

1-kings-18:12:15.summary: Samuel ministered as a child, loosely like serving the Lord from youth.

1-kings-18:12:16.summary: A king threatens death to servants who fail him, a general parallel to Obadiah's fear (range truncated).

1-kings-18:12:17.summary: “From my youth” shares the phrase of lifelong devotion to God.

1-kings-18:12:18.summary: Jesus “led up… by the Spirit” loosely parallels the Spirit carrying a prophet.

1-kings-18:12:19.summary: The fear of the Lord hates evil; general description of the God-fearer.

1-kings-18:12:20.summary: Josiah seeks the Lord “while still a boy,” loosely like fearing the Lord from youth.

1-kings-18:12:21.summary: “Who among you fears the Lord? Let him listen to His servant's voice” loosely fits Obadiah heeding Elijah.

1-kings-18:12:22.summary: Timothy knew Scripture from infancy, loosely like lifelong devotion.

1-kings-18:12:23.summary: Herod's massacre of infants has no specific link to Obadiah's fear or piety.

1-kings-18:13:1.summary: Obadiah fed hidden prophets “bread and water”; Jesus commends those who gave Him food and drink when hungry and thirsty.
1-kings-18:13:1.why: Frames feeding God’s servants as service to the Lord.

1-kings-18:13:2.summary: Paul recalls his labor and blameless conduct; nothing ties this to Obadiah hiding and feeding the prophets.
1-kings-18:13:2.why: No real link to the episode.

1-kings-18:13:3.summary: Paul’s hands supplying his companions’ needs shares only a general idea of provision with Obadiah’s feeding of prophets.

1-kings-18:13:4.summary: Jesus promises reward to whoever “receives a prophet” and gives “a cup of cold water,” matching Obadiah sheltering prophets with bread and water.
1-kings-18:13:4.why: Shows the worth of caring for God’s prophets.

1-kings-18:13:5.summary: Abimelech, like Obadiah, appeals to his own upright conduct to avoid an unjust death.
1-kings-18:13:5.why: Loose parallel of pleading one’s integrity.

1-kings-18:13:6.summary: The psalmist appeals to his righteousness and “purity of my hands,” loosely like Obadiah citing his faithful deeds.
1-kings-18:13:6.why: General appeal to a record of faithfulness.

1-kings-18:14:0.summary: Obadiah fears Ahab will kill him; Jesus says not to fear those who can kill only the body.
1-kings-18:14:0.why: Sets fear of a king against fear of God.

1-kings-18:15:0.summary: Elijah’s same oath, “As the Lord … lives, before whom I stand,” opens his first appearance to Ahab.
1-kings-18:15:0.why: Links Elijah’s signature oath across the narrative.

1-kings-18:15:1.summary: Obadiah’s own oath “As the Lord your God lives” in the same conversation prompts Elijah’s answering oath.
1-kings-18:15:1.why: Shows the exchange of oaths in this scene.

1-kings-18:15:2.summary: The psalm’s title “Lord of powers” renders the same divine title as Elijah’s “Lord of hosts.”
1-kings-18:15:2.why: Illustrates the meaning of the divine title.

1-kings-18:15:3.summary: Gabriel describes himself as one “who stands before God,” the same service idiom as Elijah’s “before whom I stand.”
1-kings-18:15:3.why: Clarifies standing before God as serving Him.

1-kings-18:15:4.summary: Isaiah’s call not to fear reproach has no specific tie to Elijah’s oath to appear before Ahab.

1-kings-18:15:5.summary: The Lord’s “powers” as ministers doing His will loosely illustrate the hosts in Elijah’s title.

1-kings-18:15:6.summary: Jeremiah condemns worship of “heaven’s host” of stars; only the word host overlaps with Elijah’s oath.

1-kings-18:15:7.summary: Hebrews discusses swearing oaths for confirmation, loosely relevant to Elijah swearing by the living Lord.

1-kings-18:15:8.summary: The call for “all His powers” to praise Him loosely reflects the heavenly hosts behind Elijah’s title.

1-kings-18:15:9.summary: The “heavenly army” praising God loosely illustrates the hosts the Lord commands.

1-kings-18:15:10.summary: The Greek-based Job text speaks of raiders and ambush, not hosts; no link to Elijah’s oath.
1-kings-18:15:10.why: Wording does not carry the assumed link.

1-kings-18:15:11.summary: Heaven and earth’s “ordered array” does not carry the title “Lord of hosts” in this reading.
1-kings-18:15:11.why: No real link in this wording.

1-kings-18:15:12.summary: Deuteronomy warns against worshiping heaven’s “adornment”; nothing connects it to Elijah’s oath.

1-kings-18:15:13.summary: Isaiah’s “Lord Sabaoth” is the same divine title as Elijah’s “Lord of hosts.”
1-kings-18:15:13.why: Connects the title used in the oath.

1-kings-18:15:14.summary: Joshua “who stands beside you” uses a similar idiom of attendance, as Elijah stands before the Lord.

1-kings-18:17:0.summary: Joshua accuses Achar of bringing destruction on Israel, loosely like Ahab blaming Elijah for Israel’s trouble; the wordings differ.
1-kings-18:17:0.why: Background on accusing someone of harming Israel.

1-kings-18:17:1.summary: Ahab again greets Elijah with hostility: “Have you found me, my enemy?”
1-kings-18:17:1.why: Shows Ahab’s settled view of Elijah.

1-kings-18:17:2.summary: Paul’s companions are accused of upsetting the world, as Elijah is accused of perverting Israel.

1-kings-18:17:3.summary: Paul and Silas are charged with throwing the city into turmoil, echoing Ahab’s charge against Elijah.

1-kings-18:17:4.summary: Paul is called a plague stirring up disturbances, a similar charge to Ahab’s against Elijah.

1-kings-18:17:5.summary: Amaziah tells Israel’s king that Amos conspires “in the midst of Israel’s house,” a parallel accusation of a prophet before Israel’s king.
1-kings-18:17:5.why: Shows a recurring pattern of blaming prophets.

1-kings-18:17:6.summary: Jeremiah is accused before the king of harming the people with his oracles, loosely like Ahab’s accusation.
1-kings-18:17:6.why: Prophets treated as enemies of the nation.

1-kings-18:17:7.summary: Jeremiah is seized and threatened with death for prophesying against the city, a general parallel to hostility toward Elijah.
1-kings-18:17:7.why: Prophets treated as enemies of the nation.

1-kings-18:18:0.summary: Azariah warns that if Judah forsakes the Lord He will forsake them, related to Elijah’s charge of “abandoning the Lord.”

1-kings-18:18:1.summary: The same charge, “they abandoned the Lord their God” and served other gods, explains Israel’s calamity.
1-kings-18:18:1.why: Matches Elijah’s diagnosis of Israel’s trouble.

1-kings-18:18:2.summary: God says “abandoning Me is bitter for you,” with “the Lord your God,” echoing Elijah’s charge.
1-kings-18:18:2.why: Shows apostasy as the true cause of trouble.

1-kings-18:18:3.summary: Ahab married Jezebel and “served Baal,” the very apostasy Elijah charges him with.
1-kings-18:18:3.why: Gives the background to Elijah’s accusation.

1-kings-18:18:4.summary: Ahab was “sold to do evil” as Jezebel turned him aside, confirming Elijah’s charge against his house.

1-kings-18:18:5.summary: Slander against the church in Smyrna has no specific link to Elijah’s rebuttal of Ahab.

1-kings-18:18:6.summary: Paul says accusers cannot prove their charges, loosely like Elijah rejecting Ahab’s accusation.

1-kings-18:18:7.summary: Paul challenges accusers to name his wrongdoing, a general parallel to Elijah turning back Ahab’s charge.

1-kings-18:18:8.summary: A general proverb that evil pursues sinners has no specific tie to Elijah’s words.

1-kings-18:18:9.summary: God makes Ezekiel’s face strong against his opponents, loosely like Elijah boldly confronting Ahab.

1-kings-18:18:10.summary: A general woe on the lawless does not connect specifically to Elijah’s charge.

1-kings-18:18:11.summary: God’s people “abandoned Me,” echoing Elijah’s charge of abandoning the Lord.

1-kings-18:18:12.summary: John rebukes a king to his face, as Elijah rebukes Ahab.

1-kings-18:18:13.summary: A general proverb on righteousness and death has no specific link.

1-kings-18:19:0.summary: Ahab “made a grove,” explaining the four hundred prophets of the groves.

1-kings-18:19:1.summary: Carmel appears only as a boundary marker in Asher’s territory.

1-kings-18:19:2.summary: Elisha later goes to “Mount Carmel,” the same mountain as the contest.
1-kings-18:19:2.why: Shows Carmel as a prophetic site.

1-kings-18:19:3.summary: Peter speaks of false prophets among the people, loosely matching the prophets of shame.

1-kings-18:19:4.summary: Carmel’s summit drying up shares the place name only, in an oracle of judgment.

1-kings-18:19:5.summary: Carmel is named as a prominent mountain by the sea, but in an unrelated oracle.

1-kings-18:19:6.summary: A queen mother patronized a grove cult, loosely like Jezebel sponsoring the groves’ prophets.

1-kings-18:19:7.summary: Jezebel learns her prophets were killed at the contest this verse sets up.
1-kings-18:19:7.why: Shows the outcome for Jezebel’s prophets.

1-kings-18:19:8.summary: Carmel’s summit is named as a hiding place; only the place name links.

1-kings-18:19:9.summary: Saul’s Carmel is a town in Judah, not Mount Carmel; only the name overlaps.
1-kings-18:19:9.why: Different place with the same name.

1-kings-18:19:10.summary: Jehu names Jezebel’s prostitutions and sorceries, the same queen who fed these prophets.

1-kings-18:19:11.summary: The false prophet is judged with the beast; loosely related to the prophets of shame.

1-kings-18:19:12.summary: The church is rebuked for tolerating “the woman Jezebel,” recalling the queen who sponsored idolatrous prophets.
1-kings-18:19:12.why: Shows Jezebel as a lasting type of seduction.

1-kings-18:19:13.summary: Elijah goes up onto Carmel after the contest, the same mountain named here.

1-kings-18:19:14.summary: “The grove stood in Samaria,” showing grove worship persisted in Israel.

1-kings-18:19:15.summary: Elijah repeats the same numbers: Baal’s “four hundred fifty” and the grove’s “four hundred” prophets.
1-kings-18:19:15.why: Same prophets in the same event.

1-kings-18:19:16.summary: Israel’s king gathers about “four hundred” prophets, a similar royal prophetic company.

1-kings-18:20:0.summary: Summoning Micaiah is a different gathering; no specific link to the Carmel assembly.

1-kings-18:21:0.summary: Jesus says no one can serve two masters, the same choice Elijah demands between the Lord and Baal.
1-kings-18:21:0.why: Gives the gospel form of Elijah’s challenge.

1-kings-18:21:1.summary: Joshua tells Israel to “choose … whom you will serve,” the Lord or other gods.
1-kings-18:21:1.why: Same demand for a decisive choice.

1-kings-18:21:2.summary: Paul says one cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons.

1-kings-18:21:3.summary: Paul asks what agreement God’s temple has with idols, a general parallel to choosing between the Lord and Baal.

1-kings-18:21:4.summary: Samuel calls Israel to remove foreign gods and “serve Him alone.”

1-kings-18:21:5.summary: Nations “feared the Lord while serving their carved images,” the very limping between two that Elijah condemns.

1-kings-18:21:6.summary: The lukewarm church, “neither cold nor hot,” resembles a people wavering between two options.

1-kings-18:21:7.summary: People swear both “by the Lord” and “by their king,” a mixed loyalty like Israel’s.

1-kings-18:21:8.summary: Deuteronomy affirms “the Lord your God, He is God,” answering Elijah’s “If the Lord is God.”
1-kings-18:21:8.why: Supplies the confession the challenge seeks.

1-kings-18:21:9.summary: The psalm says “the Lord—He is God,” echoing the issue Elijah poses.
1-kings-18:21:9.why: Supplies the confession the challenge seeks.

1-kings-18:21:10.summary: Paul says one is slave of whom one obeys, loosely related to choosing whom to follow.

1-kings-18:21:12.summary: Israel answers Joshua, “The Lord we will serve,” whereas at Carmel the people answer not a word.
1-kings-18:21:12.why: Contrasts a clear answer with silence.

1-kings-18:21:13.summary: Manasseh comes to know “the Lord Himself is God,” the conclusion Elijah urges.

1-kings-18:21:14.summary: Judah’s “What shall we answer” concerns guilt over a cup, not the people’s silence at Carmel.

1-kings-18:21:15.summary: Laban and Bethuel accepting the Lord’s command has no specific link.

1-kings-18:21:16.summary: David’s “Thou art God” in a prayer about his house has no specific tie to Elijah’s challenge.

1-kings-18:21:17.summary: The guest without a wedding garment is speechless, like the people who answer not a word.

1-kings-18:21:18.summary: Pharaoh’s refusal to know the Lord does not specifically connect to the wavering at Carmel.

1-kings-18:21:19.summary: Jesus choosing the twelve apostles has no connection to this verse.

1-kings-18:21:20.summary: A question about the greatest commandment has no specific link.

1-kings-18:21:21.summary: Job puts his hand over his mouth with no answer, loosely like the people’s silence.

1-kings-18:21:22.summary: Jesus silenced the Sadducees, loosely like the people left without a word.

1-kings-18:21:23.summary: The law stops “every mouth,” loosely like the people unable to answer.

1-kings-18:21:24.summary: Sirach warns not to approach the Lord “with a divided heart,” the wavering Elijah rebukes.

1-kings-18:21:25.summary: Woe to the sinner “who walks on two paths,” like limping on both knees.
1-kings-18:21:25.why: Same image of wavering between two ways.

1-kings-18:22:0.summary: Elijah again says “I remain utterly alone,” as here at Carmel.
1-kings-18:22:0.why: Shows Elijah’s recurring sense of isolation.

1-kings-18:22:1.summary: Elijah repeats “I remain utterly alone” at Horeb.
1-kings-18:22:1.why: Shows Elijah’s recurring sense of isolation.

1-kings-18:22:2.summary: Another prophet approaches Israel’s king, showing Elijah was not literally the only prophet.

1-kings-18:22:3.summary: Elijah had summoned the same “four hundred fifty” and “four hundred” prophets.
1-kings-18:22:3.why: Same prophets in the same event.

1-kings-18:22:4.summary: Sons of the prophets are still active in Israel, qualifying Elijah’s claim to be alone.

1-kings-18:22:5.summary: Another prophet confronts the king of Israel, showing others still served the Lord.

1-kings-18:22:6.summary: Peter warns that false prophets arise and many follow them, loosely like the many Baal prophets.
1-kings-18:22:6.why: General theme of many false prophets.

1-kings-18:22:7.summary: People heap up teachers who suit their desires, loosely like a king’s many false prophets.

1-kings-18:22:8.summary: Ben-Hadad’s servants pleading for his life has no link to Elijah’s statement.

1-kings-18:22:9.summary: Paul cites Elijah’s complaint “I alone was left,” echoing “I remain … utterly alone.”
1-kings-18:22:9.why: Shows Paul’s use of Elijah’s words.

1-kings-18:22:10.summary: The many on the broad road and the warning against false prophets loosely echo one prophet against hundreds.

1-kings-18:22:11.summary: Four hundred prophets stand against Micaiah, the one prophet of the Lord, much as Elijah stands alone against hundreds.
1-kings-18:22:11.why: Same pattern of one true prophet against many.

1-kings-18:24:1.summary: David cries to the Lord and “He answered him with fire from heaven” on the altar, the very sign Elijah proposes.
1-kings-18:24:1.why: Another time God answered by fire.

1-kings-18:24:2.summary: Fire from the Lord consumes the offering and the people fall on their faces, as later happens at Carmel.
1-kings-18:24:2.why: Precedent for God’s fire accepting sacrifice.

1-kings-18:24:3.summary: Israel sees the fire descend, falls face down, and praises the Lord, the response Elijah’s test seeks.
1-kings-18:24:3.why: Shows fire as God’s public sign.

1-kings-18:24:4.summary: At Solomon’s prayer “fire came down from heaven” and consumed the offerings.

1-kings-18:24:5.summary: Fire from the rock consumes Gideon’s offering as a sign from the Lord’s messenger.

1-kings-18:24:6.summary: The woman’s answer to David about Joab shares nothing specific with Elijah’s proposal.

1-kings-18:24:7.summary: Hezekiah calls the Lord’s word “good,” loosely like the people calling Elijah’s proposal good.

1-kings-18:26:0.summary: Idols cannot step or act, the same powerlessness as Baal’s silence.

1-kings-18:26:1.summary: Paul recalls “the mute idols,” loosely echoing Baal giving “no voice.”

1-kings-18:26:2.summary: “An idol is nothing,” explaining why Baal gives no answer.

1-kings-18:26:3.summary: Jesus warns against babbling like Gentiles who think many words get a hearing, like “Hear us, Baal, hear us!” all morning.
1-kings-18:26:3.why: Contrasts pagan repetition with true prayer.

1-kings-18:26:4.summary: Belshazzar praises man-made idols instead of the living God, a general theme of false worship.

1-kings-18:26:5.summary: Habakkuk mocks makers of “mute idols,” matching Baal’s “no voice and no hearing.”

1-kings-18:26:6.summary: Idolaters are “praying as though to gods who do not save,” exactly what Baal’s prophets do.
1-kings-18:26:6.why: Names the futility of their prayers.

1-kings-18:26:7.summary: Paul says sacrifices to idols go to demons, a general comment on pagan sacrifice.

1-kings-18:26:8.summary: The Greek-based Zephaniah speaks of judgment at the gateways, not of leaping or running about an altar.
1-kings-18:26:8.why: Wording does not carry the assumed link.

1-kings-18:26:9.summary: Sennacherib is killed while worshiping his cult-image, which does not help him.

1-kings-18:26:10.summary: Elijah’s proposal that the gods be called on and the one answering by fire is God is what Baal’s prophets now attempt.

1-kings-18:26:11.summary: Idols “have a mouth but will not speak … ears but will not listen,” as Baal gives no voice or hearing.

1-kings-18:26:12.summary: The idolater prays to his carved god, “Rescue me,” in vain, like Baal’s prophets crying out.
1-kings-18:26:12.why: Same futile prayer to an idol.

1-kings-18:26:13.summary: The nations’ idols “have ears and will not hear,” matching the absence of any hearing from Baal.

1-kings-18:27:0.summary: God taunts idols to act and prove they are gods, as Elijah mocks Baal.

1-kings-18:27:1.summary: The Lord awakes “like one sleeping” to strike His enemies, unlike Baal who never wakes.
1-kings-18:27:1.why: Contrasts the living God with Baal.

1-kings-18:27:2.summary: Ecclesiastes’ advice to the young man has no specific link to Elijah’s mockery.

1-kings-18:27:3.summary: God ironically invites Israel to its empty sacrifices at Bethel, loosely like Elijah’s sarcasm.

1-kings-18:27:4.summary: The One guarding Israel “will neither slumber nor sleep,” unlike Baal who may be asleep.
1-kings-18:27:4.why: Contrasts the true God with Baal.

1-kings-18:27:5.summary: Isaiah’s ironic commands to the nations to be strong share only a mocking tone.

1-kings-18:27:6.summary: Isaiah ridicules making a god from leftover firewood, satire of idols like Elijah’s.

1-kings-18:27:7.summary: A warning that strength comes from the Lord has no specific tie to Elijah’s mockery.

1-kings-18:27:8.summary: Jesus sleeps but awakes and rules wind and sea, unlike the sleeping Baal.
1-kings-18:27:8.why: Contrasts the true Lord with Baal.

1-kings-18:27:9.summary: The psalmist asks why the Lord sleeps, while Elijah mocks a god who may truly be asleep.

1-kings-18:27:10.summary: Micaiah’s ironic “Go up!” is another prophet’s sarcasm before a king.

1-kings-18:27:11.summary: God’s ironic command to Israel to go on with their practices shares a sarcastic tone.

1-kings-18:27:12.summary: Jesus’ “Sleep on now” to His disciples has nothing to do with mocking Baal.

1-kings-18:27:13.summary: Jesus’ “Sleep on now” in Gethsemane has no link to Elijah’s taunt.

1-kings-18:27:14.summary: Jesus’ ironic “very well indeed” shares only an ironic tone with Elijah.

1-kings-18:27:15.summary: The call “Awake, awake” to Jerusalem and God’s arm differs from mocking a sleeping Baal.

1-kings-18:28:0.summary: The Law forbids making “incisions in your body,” the very practice Baal’s prophets perform.
1-kings-18:28:0.why: Shows the rite was forbidden to Israel.

1-kings-18:28:1.summary: Deuteronomy forbids pagan mourning rites, but this Greek-based wording does not mention cutting.
1-kings-18:28:1.why: Related prohibition, weaker in this wording.

1-kings-18:28:2.summary: The demoniac “cried out and cut himself,” as Baal’s prophets cry aloud and cut themselves.
