1-kings-19:2:9.summary: “You do not know what tomorrow brings,” fitting Jezebel’s vow about tomorrow.
1-kings-19:2:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-kings-19:2:10.summary: Herod plans to kill Peter the next day, a general parallel to Jezebel’s plan.

1-kings-19:2:11.summary: The enemy boasts “I will slay with my sword,” loosely like Jezebel’s threat.

1-kings-19:2:12.summary: Sennacherib’s blasphemous arrogance is a general parallel to Jezebel’s defiance.

1-kings-19:3:0.summary: The naming of “the Well of Swearing” explains Beer-sheba, though this wording does not use that name.

1-kings-19:3:1.summary: The disciples flee in fear, loosely like Elijah fleeing for his life.

1-kings-19:3:2.summary: Peter denies Jesus out of fear after boldness, loosely like Elijah’s fear after Carmel.

1-kings-19:3:3.summary: Paul’s thorn in the flesh has no specific link to Elijah’s flight.

1-kings-19:3:4.summary: David flees to escape Saul’s hand, a general parallel to Elijah fleeing Jezebel.

1-kings-19:3:5.summary: God rebukes fear of a mortal oppressor, fitting Elijah’s fear of Jezebel.
1-kings-19:3:5.why: Fear of man versus trust in God.

1-kings-19:3:6.summary: Moses flees a ruler who seeks to kill him, a general parallel.

1-kings-19:3:7.summary: Abraham fears for his life, a general parallel to Elijah’s fear.

1-kings-19:3:8.summary: Amos is told to withdraw to Judah’s land, loosely like Elijah fleeing to Judah.
1-kings-19:3:8.why: Prophet driven from Israel to Judah.

1-kings-19:3:9.summary: “From Dan to Beersheba” names Beer-sheba as the land’s southern limit.

1-kings-19:4:1.summary: Moses asks God to “slay me outright” in his distress, as Elijah asks God to take his life.

1-kings-19:4:3.summary: Jeremiah curses the day he was born in despair, a prophet’s parallel to Elijah’s wish to die.

1-kings-19:4:4.summary: Paul weighs the desire to depart against remaining, a loose parallel to Elijah’s wish to die.

1-kings-19:4:5.summary: A man of God is found sitting under an oak, loosely like Elijah under the broom bush.

1-kings-19:4:6.summary: “Are we better off? Not at all” loosely echoes “I am no better than my fathers.”

1-kings-19:4:7.summary: Hagar in the wilderness sits apart in despair near a bush, a loose parallel.

1-kings-19:4:8.summary: Job speaks of souls in pain “who long for death,” the very wish Elijah voices.

1-kings-19:4:9.summary: Nahum’s description of Amon’s waters has no link.

1-kings-19:4:10.summary: Elijah, who asked to die, is later taken up by a chariot of fire.
1-kings-19:4:10.why: Contrasts his despair with his end.

1-kings-19:4:11.summary: Jesus, wearied from the journey, sits down, loosely like Elijah sitting exhausted.

1-kings-19:4:12.summary: Amos’s survey of kingdoms has no specific link to Elijah’s words.

1-kings-19:4:13.summary: The Father feeds the birds, foreshadowing God’s feeding of Elijah after this prayer.

1-kings-19:4:14.summary: Elijah fled for his life to Beer-sheba, from where he now goes into the wilderness.

1-kings-19:5:0.summary: “An angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear Him and will rescue them.”

1-kings-19:5:1.summary: An angel strikes sleeping Peter and says “Rise quickly,” as Elijah is touched and told “Rise.”

1-kings-19:5:2.summary: Angels are ministering spirits sent for service, as one serves Elijah here.

1-kings-19:5:3.summary: Gabriel’s report about the end of wrath has no link to Elijah’s rest.

1-kings-19:5:4.summary: Those seeking the Lord lack no good thing, loosely like Elijah being fed.

1-kings-19:5:5.summary: Gabriel approaches Daniel in prayer, a general angelic visit.

1-kings-19:5:6.summary: “I will certainly not leave you,” fitting God’s care for the despairing Elijah.

1-kings-19:5:7.summary: An angel touches the fallen Daniel and raises him, as Elijah is touched and raised.
1-kings-19:5:7.why: Same angelic touch restoring a prophet.

1-kings-19:5:8.summary: Jacob sleeps on the journey and sees angels, a loose parallel to Elijah sleeping and an angel appearing.

1-kings-19:6:0.summary: After His wilderness trial “angels came and ministered” to Jesus, as an angel feeds Elijah.
1-kings-19:6:0.why: Same angelic ministry in the wilderness.

1-kings-19:6:1.summary: Ravens brought Elijah bread and water, God’s earlier provision for the same prophet.

1-kings-19:6:2.summary: Jesus asking if the disciples have fish has no specific link.

1-kings-19:6:3.summary: The widow’s “hearth cake,” flour, and “flask” fed Elijah earlier, matching this meal.

1-kings-19:6:4.summary: “Bread will be given him, and his water is trustworthy,” matching Elijah’s provided bread and water.

1-kings-19:6:5.summary: The Father knows our needs, a general fit to Elijah’s provision.

1-kings-19:6:6.summary: Jesus fears the hungry crowd will collapse on the way, loosely like Elijah fed for his journey.

1-kings-19:6:7.summary: Jesus provides a fire with fish and bread, loosely like the meal laid at Elijah’s head.

1-kings-19:6:8.summary: Trusting the Lord leads to being fed, a general parallel.

1-kings-19:7:0.summary: The Lord pities those who fear Him, knowing we are dust, fitting His care for weary Elijah.

1-kings-19:7:1.summary: “As your days, so shall your strength be,” loosely fitting strength for the journey.

1-kings-19:8:0.summary: Moses spent “forty days and forty nights” before the Lord without bread or water.
1-kings-19:8:0.why: Links Elijah with Moses at the same mountain.

1-kings-19:8:1.summary: Moses was before the Lord “forty days and forty nights” on the mountain.
1-kings-19:8:1.why: Links Elijah with Moses at the same mountain.

1-kings-19:8:2.summary: Moses came to “Mount Horeb,” the same mountain Elijah reaches.

1-kings-19:8:4.summary: Jesus fasted “forty days and forty nights,” matching Elijah’s journey.
1-kings-19:8:4.why: Links Elijah with Jesus’ wilderness fast.

1-kings-19:8:5.summary: Jesus was in the wilderness “forty days” and angels ministered to Him, as with Elijah.
1-kings-19:8:5.why: Same pattern of wilderness and angelic aid.

1-kings-19:8:6.summary: God’s power made complete in weakness loosely fits Elijah sustained by divine food.

1-kings-19:8:7.summary: Malachi names both “Horeb” and “Elijah the Tishbite.”
1-kings-19:8:7.why: Joins Elijah and Horeb in prophecy.

1-kings-19:8:8.summary: Jesus spent “forty days” in the wilderness eating nothing.
1-kings-19:8:8.why: Links Elijah with Jesus’ wilderness fast.

1-kings-19:8:9.summary: Daniel’s friends thrive on simple food, a loose parallel to strength from food.

1-kings-19:8:10.summary: Moses abode on the mountain “forty days and forty nights” to receive the covenant.
1-kings-19:8:10.why: Links Elijah with Moses at the same mountain.

1-kings-19:8:11.summary: God descended on Mount Sinai in fire, the mountain Elijah approaches under another name.

1-kings-19:8:12.summary: Sirach says Elijah heard rebuke “at Sinai” and judgments “at Horeb.”
1-kings-19:8:12.why: Later reflection on Elijah at Horeb.

1-kings-19:9:0.summary: God’s searching question to Adam (“where are you?”) resembles the Lord’s question to the hiding Elijah.
1-kings-19:9:0.why: Shows God seeking out a person in hiding.

1-kings-19:9:1.summary: Both use a probing rhetorical question about why someone is where they are, but the settings differ entirely.
1-kings-19:9:1.why: Loose echo of God’s challenging questions.

1-kings-19:9:3.summary: Moses placed in the rock as the Lord’s glory passes parallels Elijah lodging in the cave on the same mountain.
1-kings-19:9:3.why: Links Elijah’s Horeb encounter to Moses’ vision.

1-kings-19:9:4.summary: Hagar, fleeing into the wilderness, is met with a divine question, as the fugitive Elijah is.
1-kings-19:9:4.why: Pattern of God questioning a fugitive.

1-kings-19:9:5.summary: Hebrews mentions prophets wandering in “caves”, recalling Elijah lodging in a cave.

1-kings-19:9:6.summary: Jeremiah wishes for a wilderness lodging away from his people, like Elijah’s withdrawal.
1-kings-19:9:6.why: Prophetic retreat from a faithless people.

1-kings-19:9:7.summary: Jonah flees from the Lord’s presence, while Elijah has fled to Horeb; both prophets are confronted.

1-kings-19:10:8.summary: Elijah repeats almost word for word his complaint: “most zealous for the Lord Almighty”, altars, prophets slain, “utterly alone”.

1-kings-19:10:0.summary: Jezebel “striking the Lord’s prophets” is the killing Elijah complains about.

1-kings-19:10:1.summary: The jealous God of the covenant relates loosely to Elijah’s zeal; English “jealous” and “zealous” share a root.

1-kings-19:10:2.summary: “A jealous God” forbidding idol worship loosely matches Elijah’s zeal against apostasy.

1-kings-19:10:4.summary: The shown verse is only Elijah calling the people near, with no shared complaint, zeal, or altars.

1-kings-19:10:5.summary: Elijah says “I remain … utterly alone” at Carmel, exactly as in his complaint.
1-kings-19:10:5.why: Same claim of being the lone prophet.

1-kings-19:10:6.summary: Phinehas is “zealous with My zeal” against Israel’s apostasy, the model of Elijah’s zeal.
1-kings-19:10:6.why: Biblical precedent for zeal for God.

1-kings-19:10:7.summary: Phinehas “was zealous for his God”, the same zeal Elijah claims.
1-kings-19:10:7.why: Zeal rewarded as a covenant model.

1-kings-19:10:9.summary: “A sword devoured your prophets” matches “killed Thy prophets with the sword”.

1-kings-19:10:10.summary: Shares the language of “zeal”, but for God’s house rather than against apostasy.

1-kings-19:10:11.summary: Jezebel’s death threat is the reason Elijah says “they seek my life”.

1-kings-19:10:12.summary: Jesus’ “zeal for Thy house” shares the word zeal only.
1-kings-19:10:12.why: Zeal theme carried into the Gospel.

1-kings-19:10:13.summary: Ahab’s hostility toward Elijah forms background to his complaint.

1-kings-19:10:14.summary: The devout have perished and no one acts rightly, like Elijah’s sense of standing alone.

1-kings-19:10:15.summary: Ahab searched every nation for Elijah, illustrating “they seek my life”.

1-kings-19:10:16.summary: Ephraim’s oppression and worthless pursuits share no specific element with Elijah’s complaint.

1-kings-19:10:17.summary: A prophet’s rebuke of Ahab over a released captive has no specific link to Elijah’s complaint.

1-kings-19:10:18.summary: Condemns keeping “the works of Achaab’s house”, the apostasy Elijah opposed.

1-kings-19:10:19.summary: “Zeal … melted me away, for my enemies forgot Thy words” closely matches zeal amid apostasy.

1-kings-19:10:20.summary: Micaiah is another faithful prophet in Ahab’s day, qualifying Elijah’s “utterly alone”.

1-kings-19:10:21.summary: Gathering prophets to Carmel is related narrative but shares nothing with the complaint itself.

1-kings-19:10:22.summary: Another prophet active under Ahab tempers Elijah’s claim to be alone.

1-kings-19:10:23.summary: The “sons of the prophets” show prophets surviving, contrary to Elijah’s claim.

1-kings-19:10:24.summary: A prophet brings the Lord’s word to Israel’s king, showing Elijah was not alone.

1-kings-19:10:25.summary: Elijah, “burning with zeal for the law”, is remembered for the zeal he claims here.

1-kings-19:10:26.summary: Sirach recalls Elijah acting “through his zeal”.

1-kings-19:11:0.summary: A great sweeping wind accompanies a theophany, like the wind before the Lord.

1-kings-19:11:1.summary: Fire and tempest surround God, echoing wind, earthquake, and fire before the Lord.

1-kings-19:11:2.summary: The Lord speaks through a whirlwind, whereas here He is not in the wind.

1-kings-19:11:3.summary: Violent storm imagery accompanies God’s voice, loosely like the wind and quake.

1-kings-19:11:4.summary: God’s voice shaking the earth loosely relates to the earthquake before the Lord.

1-kings-19:11:5.summary: The Lord descends on Mount Sinai (Horeb), the same mountain where Elijah stands before Him.

1-kings-19:11:6.summary: The shaking of bones in Ezekiel’s vision has no specific link to the Horeb theophany.

1-kings-19:11:7.summary: An earthquake accompanies a heavenly theophany.

1-kings-19:11:8.summary: “The earth shook … this Sinai” describes earthquake before God at the same mountain.

1-kings-19:11:9.summary: Moses is told to “stand before Me there on the mountain”, matching “stand before the Lord on the mountain”.

1-kings-19:11:10.summary: Storm, fire, and darkness at Sinai parallel the phenomena at Horeb.

1-kings-19:11:11.summary: Earth and heaven flee before God’s face, loosely like nature convulsing before Him.

1-kings-19:11:12.summary: Moses on the mountain forty days relates to the same mountain, though the source verse does not mention forty days.

1-kings-19:11:13.summary: A great earthquake is a sign of divine action.

1-kings-19:11:14.summary: God summons Moses up the mountain, a loose parallel to Elijah’s summons.

1-kings-19:11:15.summary: A great earthquake accompanies a heavenly visitation.

1-kings-19:11:16.summary: The earth shook and “the rocks split”, loosely like rocks crushed before the Lord.

1-kings-19:11:17.summary: A divine voice on “the holy mountain” loosely parallels the Horeb encounter.

1-kings-19:11:18.summary: “Not by great power or by strength” loosely echoes the Lord not being in the mighty forces.

1-kings-19:11:19.summary: Mountains shake and “rocks were crushed before Him”, matching rocks crushed “before the Lord”.

1-kings-19:11:20.summary: God’s way “in consummation and shaking” loosely matches the convulsions before Him.

1-kings-19:11:21.summary: “The Lord passed before him” at Sinai matches “the Lord will pass by”.

1-kings-19:11:22.summary: God coming from a mountain in brightness is general theophany imagery.

1-kings-19:11:23.summary: The Lord passing by Moses in the rock’s cleft parallels the Lord passing by Elijah.

1-kings-19:11:24.summary: Elijah appears with Moses on a high mountain at a theophany, recalling his Horeb meeting.

1-kings-19:11:25.summary: Sound, flashes, and a smoking mountain at Sinai loosely parallel Horeb’s phenomena.

1-kings-19:11:26.summary: An earthquake is linked to the Lord’s coming, a general shared motif.

1-kings-19:11:27.summary: Earthquakes as end-time signs share only the word with the theophany.

1-kings-19:11:28.summary: Terror and the earth astonished in battle has no real link to Elijah’s theophany.

1-kings-19:11:29.summary: Thunder, lightning, and cloud on Mount Sinai parallel the storm signs at Horeb.

1-kings-19:12:0.summary: Job hears “a breeze and a voice” with no visible form, like the gentle breeze in which the Lord comes.

1-kings-19:12:1.summary: “Not by great power … but by My Spirit” loosely matches God not being in the fire but in the breeze.
1-kings-19:12:1.why: God works quietly, not by force.

1-kings-19:12:2.summary: At Horeb Israel heard God’s voice out of fire; here the Lord was not in the fire.

1-kings-19:12:3.summary: At the same mountain the Lord spoke “out of the midst of the fire”; Elijah finds Him not in the fire.
1-kings-19:12:3.why: Highlights the new mode of revelation.

1-kings-19:12:4.summary: The Lord passing by and proclaiming His mercy loosely relates to the gentle way He comes.

1-kings-19:12:5.summary: Elihu’s promise not to overwhelm Job shares no specific element with the breeze.

1-kings-19:12:6.summary: God appears in fire at the bush on Horeb, whereas here He is not in the fire.

1-kings-19:12:7.summary: A flame and torch of fire mark God’s presence, in contrast to this fire without Him.

1-kings-19:12:8.summary: A sound like violent wind signals the Spirit, unlike the gentle breeze here.

1-kings-19:12:9.summary: God as “a consuming fire” loosely relates to the fire that precedes Him.

1-kings-19:12:10.summary: At Carmel the Lord answered by fire; at Horeb He was not in the fire.

1-kings-19:12:11.summary: Peter’s Pentecost conclusion has no specific link to the gentle breeze.

1-kings-19:12:12.summary: Elijah taken up amid fire and tumult relates to fire around his encounters.

1-kings-19:12:13.summary: Fire falls at Elijah’s word, a loose link to the fire before the Lord.

1-kings-19:13:1.summary: Elijah bowing with his face between his knees is a similar humble posture.

1-kings-19:13:2.summary: Isaiah’s dread at seeing the Lord loosely parallels Elijah covering his face.

1-kings-19:13:3.summary: Seraphim “covered their faces” before God, as Elijah covered his face.
1-kings-19:13:3.why: Covering the face in God’s presence.

1-kings-19:13:4.summary: Jesus’ repeated question to Peter loosely matches the repeated question to Elijah.

1-kings-19:13:5.summary: “My face shall not appear to you” explains why Elijah covers his face at the same mountain.

1-kings-19:13:6.summary: A divine question to the fleeing Hagar loosely echoes the question to Elijah.

1-kings-19:13:7.summary: At Horeb Moses “turned his face away, for he feared to look” before God, as Elijah covers his face.

1-kings-19:14:8.summary: Elijah’s earlier answer is repeated almost verbatim, with the same question preceding it.

1-kings-19:14:0.summary: Israel compared to one “transgressing a covenant” matches the charge of forsaking it.

1-kings-19:14:1.summary: “They did not remain in My covenant” echoes forsaking the covenant.

1-kings-19:14:2.summary: “They abandoned the holy covenant” shares the wording, though about another era.

1-kings-19:14:3.summary: “They forsook the covenant of the Lord” uses the same charge as “forsaken Thy covenant”.

1-kings-19:14:4.summary: Israel not faithful in His covenant loosely parallels forsaking the covenant.

1-kings-19:14:5.summary: “You abandoned the Lord” broadly echoes Israel’s apostasy.

1-kings-19:14:6.summary: “They abandoned the covenant of the Lord” and served foreign gods closely matches Elijah’s charge.

1-kings-19:14:7.summary: Predicts Israel will turn to foreign gods and break the covenant.

1-kings-19:14:9.summary: Watchmen on Jerusalem’s walls share no specific element with Elijah’s complaint.

1-kings-19:14:10.summary: Not keeping silent for Zion has no specific link to Elijah’s complaint.

1-kings-19:15:0.summary: God calls the foreign king Cyrus His anointed, as He orders a foreign king anointed.

1-kings-19:15:1.summary: A prophet appointed over nations and kingdoms loosely matches Elijah sent to anoint kings.

1-kings-19:15:3.summary: Names “Hazael king of Syria”, fulfilling the command to anoint him.

1-kings-19:15:4.summary: Hazael is king fighting Israel, the man Elijah was to anoint.

1-kings-19:15:5.summary: The shown text has God giving the earth and kingdoms to whom He wills; judged on truncated text.

1-kings-19:15:6.summary: Shares only the place name Damascus in an unrelated battle.

1-kings-19:15:7.summary: Judgment on “Hazael’s house” names the king Elijah is told to anoint.

1-kings-19:15:8.summary: Shares only the road to Damascus, in a different setting.

1-kings-19:15:9.summary: Sirach recalls Elijah hearing “judgments of vengeance at Horeb”, i.e., this commission.

1-kings-19:16:0.summary: Elijah finds “Elisha son of Shaphat” and throws his cloak over him, beginning the commissioning ordered here.

1-kings-19:16:1.summary: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, taking up the prophet’s role “in your place”.

1-kings-19:16:3.summary: “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest upon Elisha” confirms him as prophet in Elijah’s place.

1-kings-19:16:4.summary: Names Abel-meholah, Elisha’s hometown, in Solomon’s district list.

1-kings-19:16:5.summary: Jesus mentions “Elisha the prophet”, but only regarding Naaman.

1-kings-19:16:6.summary: Mentions “the edge of Abel-meholah”, the town named as Elisha’s home.

1-kings-19:16:7.summary: Sirach recalls Elijah anointing “kings for retribution, and prophets as successors after him”.

1-kings-19:17:0.summary: God gives Israel into the hand of “Hazael king of Syria”, the sword foretold here.

1-kings-19:17:1.summary: “Hazael afflicted Israel”, fulfilling the threat of Hazael’s sword.

1-kings-19:17:2.summary: Elisha foresees Hazael killing Israel’s men “with the sword”.

1-kings-19:17:3.summary: God slays “with the words of My mouth” through prophets, loosely like Elisha putting to death.

1-kings-19:17:4.summary: “Hazael struck them throughout Israel’s territory” fulfils Hazael’s sword.

1-kings-19:17:5.summary: Escaping a lion only to meet a bear resembles escaping one sword to fall to the next.

1-kings-19:17:6.summary: Jehu son of Nimshi conspires against Joram, beginning his sword of judgment (judged on truncated text).

1-kings-19:17:7.summary: Slaying the ungodly with the breath of his lips loosely matches prophetic judgment.

1-kings-19:17:8.summary: A prophet appointed over kingdoms to uproot and destroy loosely relates to judgment through Elisha.

1-kings-19:17:9.summary: No fighter will save his life, a general image of inescapable judgment.

1-kings-19:17:10.summary: “The rest were killed with the sword” is a general judgment image.

1-kings-19:17:11.summary: “Whoever flees the fear will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs … caught by the trap” mirrors the escape-and-catch pattern.

1-kings-19:17:12.summary: Elisha curses mockers and bears kill them, an instance of Elisha’s deadly judgment.

1-kings-19:18:1.summary: The Lord “left us seed” so Israel did not perish, like the seven thousand He leaves.

1-kings-19:18:2.summary: “Their remnant will be saved” and will trust God, echoing a preserved faithful remnant.

1-kings-19:18:3.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of cast images and sacrifice but lacks the kissing of idols the link assumes.

1-kings-19:18:4.summary: “Every knee should bend” shares knee-bending language, but toward Jesus, not Baal.

1-kings-19:18:5.summary: The Greek reading “Take hold of instruction” lacks the kiss the English label assumes.

1-kings-19:18:6.summary: Job disavows kissing his hand in secret worship, loosely like refusing homage to Baal.

1-kings-19:18:7.summary: “Every knee will bend to Me” shares knee language, but in a judgment context.

1-kings-19:18:8.summary: The command not to bow down to idols underlies refusing to bow to Baal.

1-kings-19:18:9.summary: Kings bowing to restored Zion shares only bowing language.

1-kings-19:19:0.summary: Elijah’s “sheepskin” is the same cloak he throws over Elisha.

1-kings-19:19:2.summary: God takes David from tending flocks, as Elisha is called from plowing.

1-kings-19:19:3.summary: Samuel appears “wrapped in a double cloak”, the prophet’s mantle in general.

1-kings-19:19:4.summary: Gideon is called while beating wheat, like Elisha called while plowing.

1-kings-19:19:5.summary: Elijah’s “sheepskin cloak”, which covered his face, is the same cloak cast on Elisha.
1-kings-19:19:5.why: Same mantle at Horeb and call.

1-kings-19:19:6.summary: A man who “works the earth” denies being a prophet, loosely contrasting with the plowman called to prophesy.

1-kings-19:19:7.summary: Jesus calls fishermen at work to follow, like Elisha called from plowing.
1-kings-19:19:7.why: Pattern of a call from work.

1-kings-19:19:8.summary: Moses is called while tending sheep, a general call-from-work parallel.

1-kings-19:19:9.summary: Amos was a herdsman before being called, like the plowman Elisha.

1-kings-19:19:10.summary: Sirach doubts a plowman driving oxen can become wise, while Elisha is called from the plow.

1-kings-19:20:0.summary: A disciple asks to bury his father first, as Elisha asks to kiss his father before following.
1-kings-19:20:0.why: Jesus’ call is more urgent than Elijah’s.

1-kings-19:20:2.summary: Farewell kisses for Paul echo only the kiss of parting.

1-kings-19:20:3.summary: Matthew rises from work and follows Jesus, a general call parallel.

1-kings-19:20:4.summary: The disciples “left their nets and followed”, as Elisha left the oxen to follow.

1-kings-19:20:5.summary: They “left the boat and their father and followed Him”, matching leaving oxen and father.

1-kings-19:20:6.summary: “We have left everything and followed” echoes the cost of following.

1-kings-19:21:0.summary: Oxen offered with “oxen’s equipment for wood”, as Elisha boils oxen with their equipment.

1-kings-19:21:1.summary: Onesimus serving Paul loosely parallels Elisha ministering to Elijah.

1-kings-19:21:2.summary: Mark useful “for service” loosely matches Elisha’s service to Elijah.

1-kings-19:21:3.summary: Joshua “attended” Moses, as Elisha “ministered to” Elijah before succeeding him.

1-kings-19:21:4.summary: Levi leaves everything, follows, and gives a feast, as Elisha feeds the people and follows.

1-kings-19:21:6.summary: Elijah’s earlier young attendant shows his use of a servant, not Elisha himself.

1-kings-22:22:20.summary: Satan filling a heart to lie is a general lying-spirit theme.

1-kings-22:23:10.summary: “God is not as a man, to be led astray” contrasts with deceived prophets; loose link.

1-kings-22:23:11.summary: God hardening Pharaoh’s heart is a general judicial-hardening parallel.

1-kings-22:42:1.summary: Asa's reign length and mother's name follow the same formula; different king.

1-kings-22:42:2.summary: Joram son of Jehoshaphat becomes king; mentions Jehoshaphat but concerns his successor.

1-kings-22:42:3.summary: The shown verse only records a death by Elijah's word and has no link to Jehoshaphat's age or reign.

1-kings-22:42:4.summary: Abijah's reign length and mother's name follow the same formula; different king.

1-kings-22:43:8.summary: “He did what was right in the Lord's eyes… everything his father… had done”; same evaluation formula, different king.

1-kings-22:43:17.summary: Azariah “did what was right… in accordance with everything his father” did; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:43:0.summary: Asa's heart was whole with the Lord despite high places; describes the father's way, but high places are not in the source.

1-kings-22:43:1.summary: Only about high places not removed, which the Saints source verse does not mention.

1-kings-22:43:2.summary: “Do not turn to the right or the left” loosely echoes “did not turn aside.”

1-kings-22:43:3.summary: Israel “quickly transgressed the way,” contrasting with Jehoshaphat not turning aside.

1-kings-22:43:4.summary: Asa's prayer of trust shows the father's piety; no direct link to Jehoshaphat's walk.

1-kings-22:43:5.summary: Those “turning aside into tangled ways” are led away; contrast with not turning aside.

1-kings-22:43:6.summary: Asa's later failure to trust the Lord; about the father, not Jehoshaphat's faithfulness.

1-kings-22:43:7.summary: “Do not turn aside from following the Lord”; general exhortation echoing not turning aside.

1-kings-22:43:9.summary: “Asa did what was right before the Lord,” the very way Jehoshaphat walked in.

1-kings-22:43:10.summary: Judah building high places is unrelated to the Saints source, which lacks any high-places note.

1-kings-22:43:11.summary: Asa's reform after prophecy; background on the father's way only.

1-kings-22:43:12.summary: David “did what was right… and did not turn aside”; similar evaluation wording.

1-kings-22:43:13.summary: Asa “did what was good and right before the Lord” and removed idols, describing the way Jehoshaphat followed.

1-kings-22:43:14.summary: Hezekiah's removal of high places relates to wording absent from the Saints source.

1-kings-22:43:15.summary: Asa's heart was complete though high places remained; background on the father.

1-kings-22:43:16.summary: Blessed is one who does not look toward vanities; general piety theme.

1-kings-22:43:18.summary: Jehoshaphat “walked in his father's earlier ways,” Chronicles' parallel to walking in the way of Asa.

1-kings-22:43:19.summary: Jehoshaphat directed his heart to seek the Lord and turned the people back to Him.

1-kings-22:43:20.summary: Jehoshaphat seeks the Lord with a fast and prayer; truncated range, judged on shown text.

1-kings-22:43:21.summary: Refusing to set lawless things before one's eyes; general righteousness theme.

1-kings-22:45:0.summary: Jehoshaphat goes down to the king of Israel, showing the peace between them.

1-kings-22:45:1.summary: Jehoshaphat's son married “Ahab's daughter” and walked in Ahab's way, a result of the peace with Israel.

1-kings-22:45:2.summary: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat: “do you help a sinner,” condemning his alliance with Israel's king.

1-kings-22:45:3.summary: Warning against being “unequally yoked”; a general principle applied to the alliance.

1-kings-22:45:4.summary: Joram walked in Ahab's way “because Ahab's daughter was his wife,” the fruit of the alliance.

1-kings-22:46:2.summary: “The rest of Jehoshaphat's acts” are recorded, Chronicles' parallel closing notice.

1-kings-22:46:0.summary: Same Judah annals formula for Rehoboam; different king.

1-kings-22:46:1.summary: Solomon's closing formula cites a different book; formula only.

1-kings-22:51:1.summary: Asa “slept and was buried with his fathers in the City of David. Jehoshaphat his son reigned,” framing Jehoshaphat's reign.
1-kings-22:51:1.why: Bookends Jehoshaphat's reign with his father's.

1-kings-22:51:2.summary: David buried in the City of David; same burial formula, different king.

1-kings-22:51:3.summary: Solomon slept with his fathers in the City of David; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:51:4.summary: Ahab's death and succession formula; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:51:5.summary: “Joram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah,” the successor named here.

1-kings-22:51:6.summary: Rehoboam buried in the City of David, son reigned; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:51:7.summary: Joram's reign in Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat's successor named in the source.

1-kings-22:52:0.summary: Nadab became king over Israel “in the second year” and reigned two years; same formula and length, different king.

1-kings-22:52:1.summary: Records the death of a king by Elijah's word; this is Ahaziah, though the shown verse does not name him.
1-kings-22:52:1.why: Notes how Ahaziah's short reign ended.

1-kings-22:52:2.summary: “Ahaziah his son reigned in his place,” the same succession.

1-kings-22:53:2.summary: Clinging to “the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin”; same formula for another king.

1-kings-22:53:0.summary: “He did evil before the Lord and walked in his father's way”; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:53:1.summary: Ahab sold himself to do evil “as Jezebel his wife turned him aside,” the way his son followed.
1-kings-22:53:1.why: Defines the way of Ahab and Jezebel.

1-kings-22:53:4.summary: Christ knocking at the door has no connection to Ahaziah's evil reign.

1-kings-22:53:5.summary: Judah's Ahaziah walked in Ahab's way with his mother as counselor; similar pattern, different king.

1-kings-22:53:6.summary: Walking “in the way of the house of Ahab”; same pattern, different king.

1-kings-22:53:7.summary: Judgment on Jeroboam's house; relevant to “house of Jeroboam” but not to Ahaziah directly.

1-kings-22:53:8.summary: Jeroboam's golden heifers that “became a sin,” the original sins of Jeroboam that caused Israel to sin.

1-kings-22:53:9.summary: A daughter consulting her mother about John's head is only loosely like a wicked mother's influence.

1-kings-22:53:10.summary: Jehu speaks of “Jezebel your mother” to Joram, Ahaziah's brother, naming her corrupting influence.
1-kings-22:53:10.why: Shows Jezebel's influence on her sons.

1-kings-22:53:11.summary: Ahaziah inquires of Baal Fly and is condemned by Elijah, illustrating his evil.

1-kings-22:53:12.summary: Baasha did evil and walked in Jeroboam's way; same formula, different king.

1-kings-22:54:5.summary: Israel bowed to foreign gods against the covenant; the shown portion is a general apostasy theme (range truncated).

1-kings-22:54:1.summary: God delays harm on Ahab: “in his son's days I will bring the harm,” bearing on Ahaziah's reign.

1-kings-22:54:2.summary: A people that “provokes Me”; shares the provocation theme.

1-kings-22:54:3.summary: Baasha provoked the Lord like Jeroboam's house; similar formula, different king.

1-kings-22:54:4.summary: Ahaziah sends to inquire of “Baal Fly, the god of Ekron,” showing his service of Baal.

1-kings-22:54:6.summary: Joram removed Baal's pillars, unlike his parents; contrasts with Ahaziah's Baal worship.

1-kings-22:54:7.summary: Israel “provoked Him with their practices”; general provocation theme.

1-kings-22:54:8.summary: Ezekiel's vision of the inner gate shares no specific element with Ahaziah's Baal worship.

1-kings-22:54:9.summary: A son who does not follow his father's sins contrasts with Ahaziah, who did; truncated range.
